concept.name: Coin days destroyed
concept.definition: Coin Days Destroyed (CDD) is an on-chain activity metric that weights coin movements by dormancy: each unspent coin accumulates one 'coin day' per day, and spending it destroys those accumulated days, so movements of old coins count far more than churn of young ones.
concept.intuition: Moving 10 BTC held for a decade rings a louder bell than moving 10 BTC bought yesterday — CDD measures the age-weighted significance of what moved.
concept.mechanics: CDD for a spent output = value × lifespan in days; the daily metric sums this over all spent outputs. A 2 BTC UTXO dormant 100 days destroys 200 coin days. Spikes flag long-term holders spending into strength or stress; supply-adjusted CDD normalizes for the steady growth of potential coin days as supply ages and inflates.
concept.formula: CDD = Σ (value_i × lifespan_i [days]) over outputs spent in the period.
concept.failure_modes: Exchange and custodian wallet maintenance periodically destroys huge coin days without any sale, producing false alarms; absolute CDD levels trend upward over the protocol's life, so raw values are not comparable across eras without supply adjustment.
concept.misconceptions: High CDD does not prove old holders are selling — it proves old coins moved, which may be custody reshuffling; context (exchange inflows, SOPR) is needed. Also, repeatedly moving the same coins can destroy at most one coin day per coin per day.
concept.example: Baseline BTC traffic runs under ~5M coin days destroyed daily; readings above 20M days are rare and historically appear during high-volatility episodes when large volumes of old coins move, such as cycle tops or capitulation events.

citations.source: Glassnode Docs - CDD (Coin Days Destroyed) metric guide
